claims.statement: For A = {x+i : x <= X}, |r_d| <= 1 for every admissible ideal and this is sharp, so sum_{N(d)<=D}|r_d| is of ORDER D -- the constant is 1/(2 pi) = 0.15915, not 1, see typeI-constant-is-one-over-two-pi -- and Type I holds exactly for D = o(X) = o(Q^{1/2}).
claims.notes: CONSTANT PINNED. The statement's '~ D' is an order statement; read as an equality it overstates by 2 pi. Nothing downstream moves, since the argument needs only that the sum is of order D and no constant turns D = o(X) into anything else.

claims.statement: The number of admissible Gaussian ideals of norm <= D is ~ (3/2pi) D, the residue of zeta(s)L(s,chi_4)/zeta(2s) at s=1.
d divides x+i if and only if x == r_d (mod N(d)) for a single residue r_d with r_d^2+1 == 0.

For A = {x+i}, the bilinear incidence graph OVER Z[i] contains no 4-cycle, so G(n1,n2) = #{m : mn1, mn2 in A} <= 1 for n1 != n2, with m and n ranging over IDEALS. Holds from both sides, in m and in n alike, at every split and on the full graph.
claims.notes: Scope is Z[i]. The rational graph of the same sequence is NOT C4-free -- see rational-graph-not-c4-free -- because one rational modulus merges several Gaussian ideals. Any use of this claim against a hypothesis stated over Z passes through gaussian-to-rational-bridge, which is `inferred`.

claims.statement: Hypothesis (R1) of the asymptotic sieve for primes requires x^{2/3} < D(x) < x.
claims.citation: Friedlander-Iwaniec, Asymptotic sieve for primes, Ann. of Math. 148 (1998), p.1043 (arXiv:math/9811186)

claims.statement: 'for thin sequences A one cannot expect (R) to hold with D(x) > A(x)'.
claims.citation: ASP p.1044
claims.notes: The ceiling this repo's Note B derives independently, stated by the sieve's own authors one paragraph past the hypotheses. With (R1)'s x^{2/3} < D it gives the sieve's density threshold directly: it applies only to A(x) > x^{2/3}, which ASP also state outright at p.1059 on hypothesis (9.2) ('A(x) >= x^{2/3+2eps}'). For x^2+1, A(x) = x^{1/2}, so D <= x^{1/2} < x^{2/3} and (R1) is unsatisfiable -- see asp-inapplicable. Confirmed present during a sweep applying 'pull the paragraph, not the clause' to ASP; the repo already had it.

claims.statement: x^{2/3} is the threshold below which the coefficient gamma(n,C) of hypothesis (B) is annihilated: 'd must be quite a bit smaller than N to ensure that mu(d) does not completely neutralize mu(n) ... our hypothesis (B) can be realistic only if D is somewhat larger than x^{2/3+eps}'.
claims.citation: ASP p.1045

claims.statement: The Friedlander-Iwaniec asymptotic sieve as stated cannot be applied to x^2+1: (R1) demands D > x^{2/3} while Type I caps at x^{1/2}, so the admissible range for D is empty.
claims.notes: BOOKKEEPING: this was the only `proved` claim of seventeen whose proof_site named a note but no test, which the registry's own rule forbids. The test existed all along -- test_asp_does_not_apply_to_x2plus1 asserts asp_applies('x^2+1') raises ImpossibleExponentError matching 'empty' -- it simply was not cited. The a^2+b^4 control is cited alongside it because a test that only checks the raise would pass if asp_applies raised unconditionally. (The first attempt at this citation named the test wrongly and test_named_tests_exist caught it, which is that guard doing exactly its job.)

claims.statement: Heath-Brown's density exponent alpha places the problems at alpha = 1 (Dirichlet), 3/4 (a^2+b^4), 2/3 (x^3+2y^3), and 1/2 (x^2+1).
claims.citation: Heath-Brown, Primes represented by x^3+2y^3, Acta Math. 186 (2001), p.2 of the Oxford ORA preprint

claims.statement: Heath-Brown did not use the asymptotic sieve: 'their condition (R1) is not quite met in our case ... Although it seems possible that Friedlander and Iwaniec's hypothesis (R1) might be relaxed sufficiently for our application, we have chosen instead to present our own version of the sieve argument.'
claims.citation: HB p.3

claims.statement: Heath-Brown's sequence has level of distribution X^{2-eps} for values of size X^3, i.e. x^{2/3-eps} -- short of (R1) by an epsilon.
claims.citation: HB Lemmas 2.1-2.2, p.5

claims.statement: For a^2+b^4 the level of distribution D = x^{3/4-5eps} is achieved, 'apart from the eps, the best that one can hope for'.
claims.citation: Friedlander-Iwaniec, X^2+Y^4 captures its primes, Prop. 3.5, p.962 (arXiv:math/9811185)

claims.statement: FI's Type I gain comes from applying the Davenport-Halberstam large sieve to the points nu/d with nu^2+1 == 0 (mod d), which for moduli in a short interval are spaced by 1/4D rather than 1/D^2.
claims.citation: X2Y4 Lemma 3.2 and surrounding text, p.957
claims.notes: This repo previously guessed the mechanism was Poisson summation in b. That was wrong; corrected in Note D.

claims.statement: FI prove the Type II bound B(x;N) << A(x)(log x)^{4-A} for x^{1/4+eta} < N < x^{1/2}(log x)^{-B}.
Over dyadic splits, max min(D_m, d_n) ~ sqrt(kappa) = |A|/Q^{1/2}. Measured ratio 0.85-0.92 across the family a^2+b^{2k}, k=2..6 (alpha 0.75 down to 0.583), and 1.26 for x^2+1 where sqrt(kappa)=1.
claims.notes: A degree heuristic supported across a one-parameter family, not a theorem. The C4-free lemma is the proved statement in the neighbourhood. A law fitted from finite data, not a theorem: the extrapolation from the measured range to all X is the unsupported step. Bounded from the other side by kappa-necessary-not-sufficient: at fixed density, kappa does not determine the achievable Type II range. Only the direction kappa = 1 => forest is used by Note F.

claims.statement: sum_m |sum_n mu(n) 1[mn in A]| ~ sqrt(MX) for M <= X, saturating for M >= X at DIAG = sum_x mu^2(x^2+1) d_M(x) ~ 0.253 X -- of order |A| but not |A|, see S-saturates-at-DIAG-not-at-A. Ratio to sqrt(MX) is 0.88-0.93 over X = 2e4..1e5 by direct measurement (exp02). TWO GROUPINGS, and the law differs between them. Per PROGRESSION -- one absolute value per (q,root) -- it is sqrt(MX) flat, confirmed over four decades X = 1e4..1e7 in exp05's rho = S/(pairs*sqrt(n)) and flat in M at X = 1e6 in exp16. Per MODULUS -- one absolute value per rational m, spanning all its roots, which is what ASP's (B) asks for -- inter-root cancellation at the square-root rate gives S_mu(M) ~ sqrt(MX)/(log M)^{1/4}, measured M-exponent 0.4803 against 0.5046.
claims.notes: A law fitted from finite data, not a theorem: the extrapolation from the measured range to all X is the unsupported step, and that is unchanged by anything below. The reduction that makes the range reachable is proved: mu((x^2+1)/m) = mu(m) mu(x^2+1) on squarefree values (cofactor-mobius-factors-on-squarefree-values) and mu(m) dies under the absolute value, so S_mu needs only mu(x^2+1), which sieves -- exp16 reaches X = 1e6, an order past exp02's Gaussian-incidence route. The residual non-squarefree correction is an asymptotic constant (squarefree-density-of-x2plus1-is-flat, 0.8948 flat to four places over 1e4..1e7) and so cannot move an exponent. HISTORY, kept because the wording moved twice in one day. It first cited only exp02's 2e4..1e5 -- less than one decade -- while carrying Note M's whole theta-axis argument. It was then corrected to say exp02 and exp05 measure 'the same sum', which was too strong: the absolute value sits per modulus in S_mu and per progression in exp05, and inter-root cancellation is invisible to the latter (root-grouping-splits-the-two-normalisations). The statement above now carries both groupings, because the earlier versions put the correction in these notes while the statement -- the part that gets quoted -- still said 'equivalent normalisation'.

claims.statement: In the window (B1) would require, M in (x^{1/2}, x^{3/4}), the measured bilinear sum shows no saving at all: S_mu/A(x) = 0.93, 1.00, 1.01.
claims.notes: Exact integer computation over the stated finite range; settles that range completely and implies nothing asymptotic. Independent of the fitted sqrt(MX) law: this is a direct exact computation in the window, not a consequence of the extrapolation. (An earlier version listed that dependency and the registry guard rejected it as resting a rigorous claim on a weaker one.)

claims.statement: Inside FI's proved Prop. 4.1 window the harness sees a^2+b^4 drop to S_mu/|A| = 0.16-0.52 while x^2+1 sits at 0.84-1.01; outside it both saturate. Confirms direction, not magnitude: a log-power saving is invisible over one decade.
claims.notes: Exact integer computation over the stated finite range; settles that range completely and implies nothing asymptotic.

claims.statement: Every level-of-distribution result in this literature concerns primes or smooth numbers in arithmetic progressions, where A(x) = x^{1-o(1)}; the best exponent reached is 5/8-eps. x^{7/12-eps} is Maynard (2020), not Iwaniec, whose contribution is the well-factorability of the linear sieve weights.
claims.notes: Corrected: an earlier version of this claim attributed 7/12 to Iwaniec, and justified inadmissibility by 'weights cannot lift a counting bound', which over-reaches -- sparse-moduli and signed-weight estimates evade counting bounds. The sound reason is that ASP's (R) sums absolute values over all squarefree d <= D.
claims.citation: Maynard arXiv:2006.07088 pp.2-3 (BFI 4/7; Maynard 7/12); Pascadi (Lichtman 66/107, Pascadi 5/8); Polymath 8a arXiv:1402.0811 (Zhang 1/2+1/584, Polymath 1/2+7/300)

claims.statement: Iwaniec (1978) proved that irreducible an^2+bn+c with a>0 and c odd takes P_2 values infinitely often, via a lower-bound weighted sieve; this remains the record for x^2+1. METHOD, now sourced: 'To prove this, Iwaniec obtained a new form of the error in the linear sieve, and he proved an equidistribution result about the roots of the quadratic congruence x^2 + 1 = 0 (mod m).' The equidistribution input is Lemke Oliver's condition (IV), a power saving over the trivial O_q(M) in the exponential sum sum_{M<m<M_1} sum_{G(Omega)=0 (mq)} e(h Omega/mq) -- i.e. the Weyl sum over the roots of the quadratic congruence, the same object as DFI's rho_h(n) and this repo's r_d.
claims.notes: Both statement and METHOD are now sourced -- statement from Pintz sec.19, method from Lemke Oliver's generalisation, read at source from the author's copy. Nothing about Iwaniec 1978 rests on the MSc essay any longer. Upgraded from `inferred` to `quoted`: a refereed survey stating the theorem is a better source than the MSc essay the repo had been relying on. The STATEMENT is now sourced; the METHOD remains second-hand until Iwaniec's original (paywalled) or Lemke Oliver, Acta Arith. 151 (2012) 241-261 is read. Pintz also gives the degree-uniform hierarchy: p(f) <= 4 deg f - 1 (Rademacher 1924), 3 deg f - 1 (Ricci 1936), deg f + c log deg f (Kuhn), deg f + 1 (Bukhstab 1967).
claims.citation: Pintz, 'Landau's problems on primes', J. Theor. Nombres Bordeaux 21 (2009), 357-404, section 19: 'Theorem (Iwaniec (1978)). If deg f = 2 and f(0) is odd, then p(f) <= 2. Corollary. n^2+1 = P_2 infinitely often.'; method from Lemke Oliver, Almost-primes represented by irreducible polynomials, Acta Arith. 151 (2012) 241-261, pp.1-3 (conditions (III)-(V) and Remark 3)

claims.statement: FI's Type I gain for a^2+b^4 comes from Poisson summation in the b variable.
claims.notes: Guessed by this repo, then refuted by reading X2Y4 p.957: the mechanism is a Davenport-Halberstam large sieve over the roots nu of nu^2+1 == 0 (mod d). Kept so it is not silently re-asserted.

claims.statement: The obstruction for x^2+1 is Type I, not Type II, so the bilinear programme is the wrong half.
claims.notes: Asserted in this repo, then withdrawn. ASP p.1045 shows (R1) is precisely the condition that hypothesis (B) is non-vacuous, so the two are one hypothesis and the dichotomy was malformed.

claims.statement: DFI (Ann. of Math. 141 (1995), 423-441) sec.6 is 'Combinatorial identities', not a sieve; its output Theorem S (p.437) needs Type I at D = x^{1/2-eps} and Type II over y = x^{1/3-eps}, and concludes only sum_{p<=x} c_p << eps*pi(x) -- o(pi(x)), not a log-power saving. Its Type II coefficients are NOT arbitrary: '|alpha_m| <= omega(m), |beta_n| <= 1 ... and, in our case, beta_n will be supported on primes' (p.437). The arbitrary 1-bounded version, Type I at X^{1/2}(log X)^{-C} and Type II to X^{3/8}, is Green-Sawhney's strengthening (their Lemma 3.2), not DFI's.
claims.notes: Corrects an earlier `inferred` entry that attributed Green-Sawhney's strengthened hypotheses to DFI. Obtained from the author's own scan at math.ucla.edu/~wdduke/preprints/equidistribution.pdf, independently re-fetched and verified byte-identical.
claims.citation: Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec, Ann. of Math. 141 (1995), Theorem S and coefficient class p.437, Prop. 2 p.426; Green-Sawhney arXiv:2410.04189v3 Lemma 3.2 p.9

claims.statement: x^2+1 meets DFI's Type I hypothesis, so DFI's sieve applies to it.
claims.notes: Refuted on reading DFI directly. Theorem S is normalised to x, and A = {x+i} has mass x^{1/2} inside norm bound x, so applied verbatim the hypotheses hold trivially and the conclusion is weaker than the trivial bound -- vacuous, not satisfied. What survives is narrower and is filed as dfi-lemma2-is-scale-free.

claims.statement: x^2+1 fails DFI's arbitrary-coefficient Type II hypothesis outright: worst-case theta = 1.000, 0.999, 0.999 across N(m) in [10,100), [100,1000), [1000,1682) at X = 2e4. With beta = mu the same ranges give 0.627, 0.775, 0.825.
claims.notes: Exact integer computation over the stated finite range; settles that range completely and implies nothing asymptotic.

claims.statement: Green-Sawhney prove an asymptotic for primes p^2+nq^2 with p,q prime, n = 0 or 4 mod 6; at n=4 this settles Friedlander-Iwaniec's Gaussian Primes Conjecture. Their sequence has alpha = 1 and is not thin by FI's own criterion.
claims.citation: Green-Sawhney, Primes of the form p^2+nq^2, arXiv:2410.04189v3 Theorem 1.1 p.1 and p.2; FI Conjecture 1.1, arXiv:1811.05507v1 p.3

claims.statement: Xiannan Li breaks parity below x^{2/3} unconditionally: Theorem 1 gives, for all 0 < gamma < 5/67, an asymptotic of the right order for primes x^3 + 2y^3 with y in (Y, Y(1+eta)], Y = X^{1-gamma}, so exponential density 2/3 - gamma/3, i.e. down to 43/67 = 0.641791. Merikoski reaches 5/8 CONDITIONALLY on exceptional characters. Neither reaches x^{1/2}.
claims.citation: Xiannan Li, Prime values of a sparse polynomial sequence, arXiv:2111.05403v1, Theorem 1 p.2 and the density remark p.2 (READ AT SOURCE); Merikoski arXiv:2108.01355 (NOT read -- the 5/8 figure is second-hand)
claims.notes: The Li half is now read at source and its figure is exact: 2/3 - 5/201 = 43/67 = 0.641791, which Merikoski's sparse-sets paper also quotes as X^{43/67+eps}. The Merikoski-5/8 half remains second-hand and is flagged inside the citation rather than left to the notes field. The previous citation read 'Li, as reported with Maynard ICM survey Question 21', which is not a quotation and was caught by auditing quoted claims for page/result locators.

claims.statement: Ford-Maynard Theorem 4.16 gives C^-(gamma,theta,nu) = 0 whenever gamma < 1/2 and gamma not in [theta,theta+nu]; Theorem 2.4 gives C^-(P_eps) = 0 at gamma = 1/2 with eps losses, remarking that 'one cannot hope to obtain non-trivial lower bounds on primes without some additional assumptions'. The escape named is divisor-bounded weights. This repo initially placed x^2+1 at gamma = 1/2 exactly; see x2plus1-sits-below-gamma-half, which corrects that to gamma = 1/2 - eps.
claims.citation: Ford-Maynard, On the theory of prime producing sieves, arXiv:2407.14368, Thm 2.4 p.6 and Thm 4.16 p.17
claims.notes: The gamma = 1/2 reading was wrong, and so was the correction to it: see fm-no-admissible-theta-at-density-half. Theorem 2.4 is quoted correctly here but does not apply to this sequence -- its hypothesis P in A*_2 requires nu >= 1/3 or theta + nu = 1/2, and Note F gives nu = 0. Its role on FM p.6 is the opposite of the use this repo made of it: the divisor-bounded repair of Theorem 2.4 is what rescues Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec.

claims.statement: Merikoski proves: there is a computable delta > 0 such that if |B cap [0,Y]| >> Y^{1-delta} for all Y >> 1 then there are infinitely many primes a^2+b^2 with b in B (Thm 1.1), via the lower bound of Thm 1.2 for |B| >= X^{1/2-delta}. His A(X) ~ X^{1/2}|B| = X^{1-delta}, so alpha ~ 1 - delta. B = {1} is off the chart by a power of X, not at a limit. He opens by naming this repo's problem: 'A key motivating question is Landau's fourth problem ... This is far beyond the current methods as the set is very sparse'. He also gives Li's record exactly: the sparsest polynomial sequence with primes has size X^{43/67+eps}.
claims.citation: Merikoski, On Gaussian primes in sparse sets, arXiv:2302.11331v3, abstract and Thms 1.1-1.2 pp.1-2; Li's record and the Fouvry-Iwaniec comparison p.2; Compositio Math. 161 (2025), 181-243
claims.notes: Read at source. The earlier entry paraphrased 'his large sieve needs N << X^{-eta}|B|' from a second-hand summary; the paper's own thresholds are quoted here instead. 43/67 = 0.641791 is the exact form of the 0.6418 the repo had been carrying for Xiannan Li.

claims.statement: Ford-Maynard (arXiv:2407.14368) restates or relaxes FI's hypothesis (R1).
claims.notes: Conjectured by this repo as 'the likeliest place for a restated or relaxed (R1)'. Refuted: the paper never cites ASP, never states (R1) or (B1)-(B3), and never mentions gamma(n,C).

claims.statement: No sector equidistribution result, however narrow, bears on the line Im z = 1, because sectors are two-dimensional and the line is not.
claims.notes: Asserted in Note A, then refuted: a sector anchored at arg = 0 is a horizontal strip, and Harman-Lewis harvest exactly that to get primes m^2+n^2 with n < p^0.119. The line is the width ~X^{-1/2} limit of the family, and an asymptotic there would prove Landau's fourth problem.

claims.statement: The line Im z = 1 is the width ~X^{-1/2} limit of the narrow-sector family. Unconditional asymptotics reach width X^{-3/10+eps} (Ricci), GRH reaches X^{-1/2+eps} for individual sectors, and Harman-Lewis get a lower bound at width X^{-0.381}.
claims.citation: Huang-Liu-Rudnick, arXiv:1903.04005v1 sec.1; Harman-Lewis, Mathematika 48 (2001), 119-135
claims.notes: Ricci's thesis (Univ. Michigan 1976) is unpublished; the X^{-3/10+eps} figure is second-hand from three agreeing restatements.

claims.statement: For fixed m, {n : mn in A} is the arithmetic progression n_0 + Z*conj(m), because Im(mn)=1 is a line whose homogeneous solutions are n = t*conj(m).
mu of the Gaussian ideal (x+i) equals mu(x^2+1) as an integer, since each rational prime dividing x^2+1 contributes exactly one prime ideal with the same exponent.

Up to the non-squarefree correction, the Type II sum equals sum_q |sum_{x<=X, x==r_q mod q} mu(x^2+1)| -- a Bombieri-Vinogradov statement for mu(x^2+1) in arithmetic progressions, at moduli up to X^{3/4} for a sequence of X terms.
claims.notes: The X^{3/4} range comes from DFI's Type II window, which this repo knows at two removes; if that window differs, the level changes.

claims.statement: The per-progression saving rho = S/(pairs*sqrt(n)), n the actual mean progression length, is flat in X at fixed M band: fitted rho ~ (log X)^c gives c = -0.057 with a band-phase spread of 0.19 over X = 1e4..1e7, against an iid null returning -0.002 and an injected (log X)^{-1/2} recovered as -0.482. So the PER-PROGRESSION law is sqrt(MX) with no log-power correction IN X, to a resolution of |c| <~ 0.2. Scope: this measures the X direction in the per-progression normalisation. exp16 adds the M direction in both normalisations at X = 1e6 -- per-progression flat (drift x1.032 over ten doublings), per-modulus NOT flat (x0.873, i.e. a (log M)^{1/4}).
claims.notes: Cross-checked against all admissible moduli at X <= 1e5: rho = 0.636-0.667 vs 0.64-0.73 for prime moduli, so the restriction does not distort the level. It cannot check the exponent -- half a decade is too short to fit one. Fitted at fixed M band, not fixed u -- at fixed u the finite-n dependence of rho confounds the log-power and the fit scatters from -0.31 to +0.13. An earlier run normalised by the nominal band length and reported rho ~ 0.655; corrected to ~0.72, which leaves the fitted c unchanged. Shuffle and iid controls agree with the actual value to 1-2%, so mu shows no detectable structure along these progressions. ALL-MODULI CROSS-CHECK, run at scale: every admissible modulus, X = 10^4..10^7, four decades, ending with a band of 4.3M (q,root) pairs. Mean rho per band is 0.605, 0.640, 0.635, 0.630, 0.632 for bands of 44, 430, 4294, 42988, 429684 pairs -- flat in M across four orders of magnitude and flat in X, against 0.64-0.73 for prime moduli. Fitted log-power restricted to bands with >= 10^4 pairs: c = -0.032 and +0.016, i.e. c = 0 to about +-0.05, tighter than and independent of the prime-moduli -0.057 +- 0.19. The apparent drift in sparse lanes is SAMPLING NOISE, diagnosed rather than assumed: sd(rho)*sqrt(pairs) = 0.60, 0.85, 0.79 for the three bands with eight X-values each, constant to 20% while the pair count varies by a factor of 100. SCOPE MADE EXPLICIT. This claim and root-grouping-splits-the-two-normalisations read as contradictory -- one says 'no log-power correction', the other measures (log M)^{1/4} -- and they are not: this one is the X direction in the PER-PROGRESSION grouping, that one is the M direction and the discrepancy is entirely PER-MODULUS. The coherent picture is S_prog ~ sqrt(MX) flat in both X and M, and S_mu = S_prog / sqrt(mean roots per modulus) ~ sqrt(MX)/(log M)^{1/4}. ASP's (B) asks for the per-modulus one, so the sieve-relevant law carries the log factor and this claim's headline never applied to it.

claims.statement: At X = 1e6, rho computed on the actual mu(x^2+1) agrees to within 1-2% with both a shuffled control (same values, random order) and a synthetic iid +-1/0 control at the same density, in every M band tested.
claims.notes: A negative result: no obstruction is visible in the correlation structure. It does NOT say mu is random, and truth is not provability -- the parity barrier is about the latter. Exact computation at one X.

claims.statement: DFI's Lemma 2 (p.436) assumes only (27) sum_{n==0(d)}|c_n| <= gamma(d)X with gamma submultiplicative and (29) gamma(p) <= c/p, so it applies to a thin sequence with gamma(d) = rho(d)/d and X ~ x^{1/2}. The Type I and Type II hypotheses must then be re-normalised to X = |A|, demanding cancellation of size |A|(log)^{-B}.
claims.citation: Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec, Ann. of Math. 141 (1995), Lemma 2 p.436, conditions (27) and (29)
claims.notes: Neither DFI nor Green-Sawhney writes the thin-sequence version down. The re-normalised level is where Note F's C4-free obstruction bites, and is the first place the repo's obstruction and the literature's machinery are in the same normalisation.

claims.statement: DFI's equidistribution theorem is for f(X) = aX^2+2bX+c with D = ac-b^2 > 0; a=1,b=0,c=1 gives D=1, so nu^2+1 == 0 (mod p) is literally covered. Their rho_h(n) = sum_{f(nu)==0 (n)} e(h nu/n) is the Weyl sum over this repo's residues r_d. Proposition 1 (p.425) bounds L_d(M) = sum_{M<m<=2M} rho_h(dm) << (h,d)^{1/20}(d/M)^{1/20}M^{1+eps}, uniformly in d up to d ~ M.
claims.citation: Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec, Ann. of Math. 141 (1995), Theorem p.424, Proposition 1 p.425, Proposition 2 p.426
claims.notes: Directly about this repo's admissible-ideal residues, and Note J reduces the Type II input to a statement about exactly these residues in progressions. BUT Proposition 1 bounds a SIGNED sum over m, and exp07 shows the difficulty is entirely in the absolute values -- so it is the right object in the wrong norm. Downgraded from 'sharpest open question' accordingly; it could still be an ingredient in an argument that handles the |.| by other means.

claims.statement: Ford-Maynard, p.2, quoting Selberg [28]: 'whenever nu = 0, there are examples of a_n with b_n = 1 for all n which satisfy (I) for arbitrary gamma < 1 but with sum_p a_p = 0, so non-trivial Type II information is necessary to detect primes'. Their Theorem 2.1 (p.3) is the quantitative version: for all gamma < 1 there is nu_0(gamma) > 0 with C^- = 0 whenever nu <= nu_0(gamma).
claims.citation: Ford-Maynard, arXiv:2407.14368v1, p.2 (Selberg [28]) and Theorem 2.1 p.3
claims.notes: This entry is now the QUOTE only. Applying it to x^2+1 needs nu = 0 for this sequence, which is c4-free plus gaussian-to-rational-bridge -- the latter `inferred`. The claim used to assert 'which Note F proves for this sequence' inside a `quoted` entry, which is exactly the conflation the registry exists to prevent: their (II) quantifies over rational m, n, and Note F's lemma is about Gaussian ideals. C^- = 0 is a statement about what these axioms can prove -- there exists an admissible sequence with no primes -- NOT about whether x^2+1 is prime infinitely often. Do not conflate.

claims.statement: Ford-Maynard's (I) demands a log-power saving at level exactly x^gamma. Note B gives Type I for D = o(x^{1/2}) and failing at x^{1/2}, so x^2+1 is at gamma = 1/2 - eps for every eps, never gamma = 1/2 -- i.e. inside the P_eps regime that their Theorems 2.4 and 4.16 kill, not the gamma = 1/2 case where they assert C^{+-} = 1.
claims.citation: Ford-Maynard, arXiv:2407.14368v1, hypothesis (I) p.2, Theorem 2.4 p.6, Theorem 4.16 p.17
claims.notes: Refuted on the third reading of arXiv:2407.14368v1, for the attribution rather than the placement. Theorem 2.4's hypothesis is P in A*_2 = {(1/2,0,nu) : 1/3 <= nu < 1/2} union {(1/2,theta,1/2-theta) : 0 <= theta <= 1/3} (p.6); this sequence has nu = 0 and is in neither component, so Theorem 2.4 never applied. Theorem 4.16 does apply on the strict reading gamma < 1/2. But the gamma = 1/2 vs 1/2 - eps distinction was never load-bearing: FM's Table 1 caption reads 'epsilons omitted', so by that standard every entry including Friedlander-Iwaniec's x^{3/4-5eps} sits at gamma = level - eps. The conclusion C^- = 0 survives by Selberg / Theorem 2.1, which turn on nu = 0 and not on gamma at all.

claims.statement: Divisor-boundedness does not exempt x^2+1: Ford-Maynard Theorem 2.7(c) gives C^-(1/2,0,nu) = 0 = C^-_bd(1/2,0,nu) at nu = 0.1616, and C^-_bd(1/2,0,3/19) = 0. The divisor-bounded escape buys nothing once nu is small, whatever the density.
claims.citation: Ford-Maynard, arXiv:2407.14368v1, Theorem 2.7(c) p.8
claims.notes: Answers the [VERIFY] this repo carried as 'the sharpest live question'. The answer was first recorded as 'the indicator weight IS divisor-bounded, and it does not help' -- true of the RAW indicator, but not of anything (4.1) admits, so read the sharpening below before quoting it. SHARPENED, and the reason recorded here was not the strongest one. FM p.13 (4.1) puts TWO conditions on the C_bd class -- |w_n| <= tau(n)^rho and sum_p b_p >= x/(rho log x) -- and the second forces b, hence a, to have mass ~ x. So C_bd is a class of DENSE sequences and x^2+1 is not in it under any normalisation: scaled to mass x the weights are ~x^{1/2} and fail the first condition, unscaled they fail the second. The conclusion (the divisor-bounded escape buys nothing here) is unchanged and now holds a fortiori -- the escape is unavailable because the hypothesis fails, not only because Theorem 2.7(c) drives the constant to 0. See fm-divisor-bounded-class-is-dense.

claims.statement: The repo's beta = mu cancellation is arithmetic information not expressible as Ford-Maynard's (I)/(II) with arbitrary coefficients -- new ONLY because it holds on ranges where the arbitrary-coefficient hypothesis fails outright, which by Note F is every range. Ford-Maynard expect specialised-coefficient results to upgrade to full ones (footnote 1, p.3); Note F proves that here they cannot.
claims.notes: Inferred, not quoted: Ford-Maynard never discuss x^2+1 and the paper contains zero occurrences of 'Landau', 'x2+1', 'Gaussian' or 'quadratic polynomial'. A mu-restricted Type II is WEAKER than the arbitrary-coefficient one at the same range, so restricting coefficients is not per se an escape; the argument only works in the narrow form stated. An earlier version of this claim rested on a truncated quotation that omitted 'although often the methods generalize to give (II)'.

claims.statement: The Type II difficulty for x^2+1 is entirely in the absolute values. At X = 3e6 the signed sum |sum_q sum_{x==r_q (q)} mu(x^2+1)| is 0.4-1.9% of the absolute-value sum sum_q |...|, and is itself below sqrt(terms). Taking |.| per modulus IS taking the sup over signs, i.e. an arbitrary outer coefficient, which is exactly what Note F's C4-free lemma proves the sequence cannot support.
claims.notes: A measurement of Note F rather than a restatement of it: the two notes describe one obstruction from two sides. Exact computation at one X. Consequence: DFI's Proposition 1 bounds a SIGNED sum over the same residues, so it is the right object in the wrong norm -- see dfi-equidistribution-covers-nu2plus1. SCOPE, added later: absolute values are not intrinsically the problem -- BV in that norm is known for mu on the density-1 sequence (bv-in-absolute-value-known-for-mu). The difficulty is the absolute values FOR THIS SEQUENCE, and the reason is the composition with a quadratic; see mu-of-quadratic-is-not-multiplicative. And the route out is now closed at the other end too: well-factorable-trades-away-the-absolute-value shows every BFI-line theorem buys its level by giving up |.|, so beyond level 1/2 there is no absolute-value statement to appeal to.

claims.statement: DFI's proof is spectral and reaches the roots of nu^2+1 == 0 directly, via Poincare series and the spectral expansion in Maass cusp forms and Eisenstein series -- 'roots of the congruence to the spectrum of the Laplacian without passing through Kloosterman sums along the way'. Its output is Proposition 1, a bound on the SIGNED sum L_d(M). DFI also state that Selberg's eigenvalue conjecture would give sharper estimates but 'the same range of uniformity', which is the axis this repo needs.
claims.citation: Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec, Ann. of Math. 141 (1995), p.426 (the quoted sentence, immediately after Prop. 2) and p.429 (spectral decomposition in Maass cusp forms u_j and Eisenstein series E_a)
claims.notes: Corrects Note G, which had assumed the spectral route was inapplicable because dispersion produces no Kloosterman sums here. True of dispersion, false of spectral methods. But spectral is not an independent option: it is the engine behind Prop 1, so it inherits the wrong-norm problem measured in exp07. Page reference corrected from 427 to 426 after reading the scan's page IMAGES rather than its OCR layer; p.429 verified and correct. The quoted sentence sits on p.426 between Proposition 2 and the start of sec.2 'Basic facts about quadratic forms'.

claims.statement: Merikoski (2022) proves sum_{p<=X} #{p = a^2+(b^2+1)^2} asymptotic to X^{3/4}/log X -- a lower bound of the correct order, NOT an asymptotic formula. Type I to D <= X^{3/4-eta'} (Prop. 4); Type II for X^{1/4+eta} << N << X^{1/3-eta} (Prop. 12), against Friedlander-Iwaniec's X^{1/4+eta} << N << X^{1/2-eta}. Coefficients: alpha(m) bounded and arbitrary, beta(n) bounded with the Siegel-Walfisz property (4.1), reduced to Siegel-Walfisz with main term 0 (4.2) by a device of Heath-Brown.
claims.citation: Merikoski, The polynomials X^2+(Y^2+1)^2 and X^2+(Y^3+Z^3)^2 also capture their primes, arXiv:2112.03617v2, Thm 1 p.2, Prop. 4 p.7, (4.1) p.14, Prop. 12 p.15, Prop. 13 p.16
claims.notes: The fourth published sequence with a known outcome. Its density is identical to a^2+b^4 by construction, so it varies structure while holding density fixed. Merikoski p.6 defines rho_1(d) = #{nu (d) : nu^2+1 = 0 (d)}, which is this repo's rho.

claims.statement: The +1 desingularises the Type II curve and that cuts both ways. Main term: for a != 0,1 the homogenisation (1-a)x_0^2 + x_1^2 - a x_2^2 is non-singular, so Weil gives eps_p(a) << p^{1/2} and the divisor sum truncates at d <= log^{2C}X -- 'having (b^2+1)^2 rather than b^4 turns out to be a friend rather than an enemy'. Error term: on the non-singular curve S(a,h1,h2;Delta) << |Delta|^{1/2+eps} << N^{1/2+eps}, 'sufficient provided that N << X^{1/3-eta}', where FI's singular curve gives S_FI << N^eps, 'which is why for a^2+b^4 one can handle the Type II sums up to N << X^{1/2-eta}'.
claims.citation: Merikoski, The polynomials X^2+(Y^2+1)^2 and X^2+(Y^3+Z^3)^2 also capture their primes, arXiv:2112.03617v2, pp. 4-5 and Section 5 p.16
claims.notes: Both halves of the trade run through the Poisson sum over b1, b2 with B1,B2 << X^{1/4}. Neither survives B = 1. So this is not a route for x^2+1; it is the mechanism that explains why kappa alone cannot predict the Type II range.

claims.statement: At Q = 10^7, a^2+b^4 and a^2+(b^2+1)^2 agree in |A| to 0.02%, in kappa to 0.04% (2368.2 vs 2367.2) and in max-over-splits min(D_m,d_n) to 2.7% (41.22 vs 40.12), and both have 4-cycles. The literature separates them by 1/6 in the Type II exponent and by asymptotic vs lower-bound. So kappa > 1 is necessary for a usable Type II range and is not sufficient.
claims.notes: The first control in this repo that varies structure at fixed density; every earlier comparison varied both together. Downgrades how much weight Notes D and F may put on kappa. The direction Note F actually uses -- kappa = 1 implies a forest implies no main term -- is unaffected.

claims.statement: For A = {a + f(b)i} with a << Q^{1/2} and b << B, |A| ~ Q^{1/2}B so kappa = |A|^2/Q = B^2 identically, and sqrt(kappa) = B is the range of the Poisson summation variables in the Type II reduction. Merikoski p.4 states the identification directly: 'For Delta != 0 applying the Poisson summation formula to the sums over b_1 and b_2 we get a main term ... N(a; Delta) := B_1 B_2 / Delta^2 |{...}|', with the ranges given as 'for any B_1, B_2 << X^{1/4}' at alpha = 3/4. For x^2+1, B = 1: Poisson summation over one point is the identity, so there is no main term to evaluate and no exponential sum to bound.
claims.notes: kappa = B^2 is arithmetic. CORRECTED: an earlier version of these notes said the identification of B with the Poisson range 'is this repo's reading of Merikoski p.4 and is not stated anywhere in the literature'. It IS stated -- p.4 says Poisson is applied to the sums over b_1 and b_2, and the resulting main term carries B_1 B_2 explicitly. What remains inferred is only the GENERALISATION to arbitrary A = {a + f(b)i} and the identification of B with sqrt(kappa); the Poisson step itself is quoted. Found by applying 'pull the paragraph, not the clause' to Merikoski -- the fourth time in one session, and the first where the fuller text STRENGTHENED a claim rather than correcting one. The same passage supplies the mechanism Note K already records: Weil on the shifted curve gives |Delta|^{1/2+eps}, sufficient only to N << X^{1/3-eta}, against N^eps on FI's homogeneous one, which is why a^2+b^4 reaches X^{1/2-eta}.

claims.statement: Ford-Maynard name Note F's counting function as the barrier: 'Showing one can take theta + nu >= 1 - 2c is closely related to estimating #{n : nm_1, nm_2 in J} with an error term better than O(1) on average over m_1, m_2 ~ x^{1-2c+eps} (i.e. to show bilinear cancellation in the error term), which is typically very difficult outside of special situations.' That is G(n_1,n_2) with the variables named the other way.
claims.citation: Ford-Maynard, On the theory of prime producing sieves, arXiv:2407.14368v1, footnote 2 p.7
claims.notes: External evidence that Note F measures the right object; Note F was derived from the Z[i] structure, not read out of a paper. Where they say 'typically very difficult', Note F proves the count is 0 or 1, so the error term IS O(1) and no averaging helps.

claims.statement: Ford-Maynard's Table 1, caption 'Examples from the literature (epsilons omitted)', lists eight successful (gamma, theta, nu). Every one has nu > 0. The smallest nu is JIA at (19/28, 9/28, 1/28); then Merikoski Thm 2 at (5/6, 1/6, 1/18), Maynard at (16/25, 9/25, 1/16), and Merikoski Thm 1 at (3/4, 1/4, 1/12) fourth. CORRECTED: this claim previously said Merikoski Thm 1 was the smallest, which is false -- three entries are smaller. Read off the table at source (p.3): Friedlander-Iwaniec (3/4,1/4,1/2), Heath-Brown (2/3,1/3,1/3), Jia (19/28,9/28,1/28), Maynard (16/25,9/25,1/16), Merikoski Thm 1 (3/4,1/4,1/12), Merikoski Thm 2 (5/6,1/6,1/18), Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec (1/2,0,1/3), Sarnak-Ubis (1/2,0,1/5). Friedlander-Iwaniec are at (3/4, 1/4, 1/2) and Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec at (1/2, 0, 1/3). So gamma = 1/2 is not fatal in itself -- with nu = 1/3 and divisor-bounded weights it works, and FM p.6 says so: 'This was exploited in Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec [7] in the case theta = 0, nu = 1/3'.
claims.citation: Ford-Maynard, On the theory of prime producing sieves, arXiv:2407.14368v1, Table 1 p.3 and p.6
claims.notes: nu = 1/12 suffices for a lower bound via Harman's sieve, so the bar is not a wide arbitrary-coefficient Type II range; it is nu > 0. Note F gives nu = 0 here. The 'smallest' figure was wrong for as long as this claim has existed and nothing depended on it: the argument needs only that every entry has nu > 0 while this sequence has nu = 0, which is unaffected. Caught by an audit agent reading Table 1 rather than the claim about it.

claims.statement: x^2+1 has no admissible Ford-Maynard parameter triple. For J of size x^{1-c}, FM p.7: 'one can only hope for (I) to hold for gamma < 1 - c and (II) for theta > c'; and (1.1) p.1 requires 0 <= theta < 1/2. At density x^{1/2}, c = 1/2, so (II) needs theta > 1/2 and (1.1) needs theta < 1/2. Computed by x2plus1.exponents.ford_maynard_theta, which raises at alpha = 1/2 and returns [1/4,1/2) at alpha = 3/4 and [1/3,1/2) at alpha = 2/3.
claims.notes: The deduction is the repo's; FM state the two ingredients but never draw the conclusion for c >= 1/2, and 'one can only hope' is an informal remark inside their discussion of the family P_theta, not a theorem. What it replaces is the gamma = 1/2 - eps argument, which turned on a distinction FM's own Table 1 caption discards. Also worth noting: their 'gamma < 1 - c' is Note B's ceiling, reached independently.

claims.statement: The incidence graph of A = {x^2+1} over Z is NOT C4-free, unlike its Z[i] counterpart. Explicit: n1 = 1189, n2 = 71978 share the moduli m = 65 and m = 109, with 65*1189 = 278^2+1, 65*71978 = 2163^2+1, 109*1189 = 360^2+1, 109*71978 = 2801^2+1. The mechanism is row merging: 65 carries four Gaussian ideals (roots 8,18,47,57) where the Gaussian graph keeps them apart. Equivalently a rational 4-cycle IS a multiplicative coincidence (x1^2+1)(x4^2+1) = (x2^2+1)(x3^2+1) -- a1a4 and a2a3 of equal norm without being associates, which Note F's lemma does not exclude and cannot.
claims.notes: Not a refutation of c4-free, which is proved and true over Z[i]. It is a statement of that claim's SCOPE. Conjugation alone does not explain the coincidences either: of 504 with x <= 1200, only 332 have a1*conj(a4) ~ a2a3.

claims.statement: Over Z the max off-diagonal Gram entry is 2 on every dyadic window [M,2M), uniformly for X <= 8000, while the full graph grows: 6, 7, 7, 8, 9 at X = 500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000. Multiplicative coincidences are sparse -- excess representations 131, 256, 497, 916 at X = 300, 600, 1200, 2400, against X^2/2 pairs.
claims.notes: AUDIT DONE, and this was the only case. Four claims quantify over 'every window': this one; full-graph-growth-is-pell and one-solution-per-class-per-window, both of which are ratio-based by construction (consecutive moduli spaced by phi^4 = 6.854 and by eps^2 respectively, so 'at most one per window' follows from the spacing and needs no sweep at all); and the-c4-free-input-is-available-in-both-rings, which cites the rewritten exp24. The doubling loops remaining in exp15, exp16, exp20 and exp24 choose which bands to REPORT in a survey, not which windows a maximum ranges over, so they carry no universal claim. THE CITED SWEEP IS WEAKER THAN THE WORDING, and the stronger version has now been checked. exp09 sweeps `M = 2; while M <= cap: ...; M *= 2` -- windows ANCHORED at powers of two -- while 'every dyadic window [M,2M)' means every M. The gap is real: [8,16) and [16,32) between them miss the pair (9,17), which is exactly how a line-family sweep passed on a counterexample at c = 6 (see the-gaussian-to-rational-transfer-fails-at-c-equals-six). Checked directly by ratio at X = 500, 1000, 2000, 4000: max Gram is 2 under BOTH criteria, so the conclusion is unaffected and only the evidence for it was narrower than stated. Pinned in tests/test_note_o.py::test_windowed_gram_bound_holds_for_UNANCHORED_windows_too. Note O's own triple work was never affected -- it uses m_{i+2}/m_i < 2, which is the unanchored criterion. The excess roughly doubles as X doubles (ratios 1.95, 1.94, 1.84), consistent with ~X over the measured range, but the implied exponent drifts 0.96 -> 0.88 and NO asymptotic law is claimed -- that would be `extrapolated` and this is not. Reproduced independently by a second session before recording. ANCHORING AUDIT, found independently by both sessions within minutes. The cited experiment exp09 sweeps `M = 2; while M <= cap: ...; M *= 2` -- windows ANCHORED at powers of two -- while this claim's wording is 'every dyadic window [M,2M)'. Those differ: [8,16) and [16,32) between them miss the pair (9,17). Re-measured by RATIO at X = 2000 and 4000: max off-diagonal Gram is 2 under both criteria, and the degree ladder is unaffected (x^2+1 and x^2+x+1 give 2, x^3+2 and x^4+1 give 1). So the conclusion stands and only the evidence was narrower than the wording. AND THE WITNESS IMPROVES: the recorded one, (1,41) with moduli 730 and 1370, uses the UNIT cofactor, which a reader can dismiss since no Type II hypothesis admits it. The same four values factor as (2,82) with moduli 365 and 685 -- 2*365 = 730 = 27^2+1, 82*365 = 29930 = 173^2+1, 2*685 = 1370 = 37^2+1, 82*685 = 56170 = 237^2+1 -- a unit-free witness for the same 4-cycle. Its cofactor ratio is 41, far above O.12's 4.7913, so it is consistent with the banded theorem rather than in tension with it.

claims.statement: The full rational graph's Gram maximum is attained at (n1,n2) = (1,5), and G'(1,5) counts solutions of y^2+1 = 5(x^2+1), i.e. the Pell equation y^2 - 5x^2 = 4, whose solutions are x = F_{2k}, y = L_{2k}. Consecutive moduli m = x^2+1 = 2, 10, 65, 442, 3026, ... have ratios converging to phi^4 = 6.8541, so at most one lies in any dyadic window. That is why the full graph grows like log X while every window stays bounded.
claims.notes: The Pell identity is arithmetic and depends on nothing measured; the measurement in rational-gram-bounded-on-windows is what pointed at the pair, not what supports the claim. (The dependency guard rejected the other ordering, correctly.) n1 = 1 cannot occur in a Type II hypothesis, where both variables are confined to ranges, so the log-growth is an artefact of admitting a unit cofactor -- which makes the windowed statement the faithful one rather than a patch. CONSTANT PINNED, on the sweep for order-statements read as equalities: the growth is G'(1,5) = log X / log(phi^2) + O(1), slope 1.0390, with the offset between -0.96 and -0.18 over X = 500 .. 1e6. Unlike the other three instances found by that sweep -- 2.41 against 1, 0.253 against 1, 1/(2pi) against 1 -- the constant here is near enough to 1 that the loose reading misleads nobody, so the category does NOT apply. Recorded because 'it does not apply here' is only worth saying with the number attached. The same computation reproduces the repo's recorded full-graph maxima 6, 7, 7, 8, 9 at X = 500..8000 from the Pell family directly.

claims.statement: The step from c4-free (a statement about Z[i]) to nu = 0 in Ford-Maynard's sense (a statement about Z, where their (II) is quantified over rational m, n) is an inference, not a proof. What is proved over Z[i] is G <= 1; over Z, on the configuration Ford-Maynard's (II) actually quantifies over -- m and n EACH banded, which is where their footnote 2 averages -- Theorem O.12 proves G' <= 1 for all X, matching the Z[i] bound exactly. (Off that configuration, with cofactors ranging freely, G' <= 2 remains measured rather than proved, and (1,41) sharing 730 and 1370 is a genuine G' = 2 -- but 41/1 is nowhere near one band, so a Type II hypothesis never sees it.) Both give no main term, so the conclusion is unchanged and only the constant moves -- but the transfer is reasoning.
claims.notes: UPDATED: the missing input has been found and it is weaker than hoped. Dickson bounds the class count by 2^{omega(|a-b|)+O(1)} = O_eps(|a-b|^eps), so the bridge closes with G' << |n1-n2|^eps on a dyadic window rather than with the measured constant 2. That is still no main term -- which is all dispersion needs -- but the step from 'O(N^eps), unstructured' to 'no main term' is reasoning, not Dickson. The remaining gap is now specific: why the measured constant is 2 when the proof allows N^eps. See classes-separate-across-windows, which measures that the classes separate. ANSWERED, the sub-gap only: 'why is the measured constant 2 when Dickson allows N^eps' is not the load-bearing part, and it now has a mechanism. Dickson bounds the number of CLASSES; what a dyadic window sees is the number of classes with a representative IN that window, and Prop L.1's spacing puts at most one member of each class in a window. So the windowed count is the number of distinct orbits meeting the window. rational-graph-contains-K-s-2 shows this concretely: the modulus pair {10,17} has infinitely many shared cofactors, in two orbits spaced by (eps^2)^2 = 459682, so a window meets one from each and the count is 2. The unwindowed count is unbounded and the windowed one is 2 for the same reason. What remains inferred is the OTHER component -- the transfer from 'no main term over Z' to 'nu = 0 in FM's sense', which is about what their (II) quantifies over and is untouched by the constant. See triple-question-upgrades-status-not-conclusion, which draws that line explicitly. QUANTITATIVE HALF CLOSED by the parallel session's Theorem O.12, verified here independently: cofactors within u = n_2/n_1 <= (5+sqrt 21)/2 = 4.7913 share at most one modulus per dyadic window, so a single dyadic band (u < 2) is C4-free with 2.4x margin. Derivation checked from scratch -- tau increases in |V| and |V| >= 1 gives tau_V >= sqrt(1+s^2) + s with s = sqrt(D)/M, and tau(1)^2 < 3 forces s < 1/sqrt 3, i.e. M/sqrt(D) = (u-1)/sqrt(u) > sqrt 3, i.e. u^2 - 5u + 1 > 0 -- and measured: banded max Gram 1 over 530,837 pairs at X = 3000 and 2,126,758 at X = 6000, free max 2, zero violations of the exact threshold. So the sentence 'proved <= 1 over Z[i] but only measured <= 2 over Z' no longer has a discrepancy OR a finite floor on the configuration that matters. WHAT REMAINS IS UNCHANGED and is the whole of this claim's `inferred` status: the step from 'no main term either way' to 'nu = 0 in their sense' is reasoning about what their (II) is quantified over, and O.12 does not touch it. It removes the numerical gap, not the argument. EVIDENTIAL BASE WIDENED, by the parallel session drawing a consequence of the c-family work that I did not: `kappa-counts-lines-and-c4-freeness-permits-one` proves A_c is C4-free over Z[i] for EVERY c, so c = 2,3,4,5 are four further instances of exactly the configuration this claim describes -- Z[i] side proved, Z side not -- and in all four the banded max Gram over Z is 1 and the free max Gram is 2, with 0 banded pairs sharing two out of 496,495 / 392,970 / 648,160 / 146,128. Before this the transfer had been tested only on the single case it was formulated from, which is the kind of evidential base that reads as strong until it is counted. Evidence for the TRANSFER only: the inference from 'no main term either way' to 'nu = 0 in their sense' is about what (II) quantifies over and no amount of c touches it. RESIDUAL DISCHARGED: the phrase in this claim's own statement -- 'the configuration Ford-Maynard's (II) actually quantifies over -- m and n EACH banded' -- was the reading this bridge carried, and it is now verified at source rather than read off. See fm-configuration-is-doubly-banded-at-source: the shared variable is confined to a factor-2 window by FM's own 'J subset (x/2, x]' (p. 7), the pair is banded by footnote 2's own 'm1, m2 ~ x^{1-2c+eps}', and (II)'s arbitrary divisor-bounded coefficients let one set xi_m = 0 off [M,2M) and kappa_n = 0 off [N,2N), so (II) implies every doubly-banded restriction of itself. The status here stays `inferred` because the transfer this claim is named for -- Z[i] C4-freeness to nu = 0 in FM's axioms -- is a different sentence, and because the count-to-nu step rests on the source's own 'closely related to'. What has gone is the part that was ours to settle.

claims.statement: For A = {f(x) : x <= X} with deg f = d, Q ~ c X^d and |A| = X, so alpha = 1/d and kappa = |A|^2/Q = X^{2-d}/c. The exponent depends only on the degree. Hence kappa > 1 only at d = 1, kappa = 1 exactly at d = 2, and kappa < 1 for every d >= 3 -- x^2+1 is the least degenerate member of a degenerate class, not a special case, and d = 1 (Dirichlet) is the only single-variable degree with bilinear structure. Measured max Gram at X = 4000, sweeping dyadic windows: 32 for 2x+1, 2 for x^2+1 and x^2+x+1, 1 for x^3+2 and x^4+1.
claims.notes: The exponent half is arithmetic and proved; the Gram column is measured at fixed X across degrees, not extrapolated in X. The ladder recovers the solved case at d = 1, which is the check that matters -- a classification that did not return Dirichlet there would be evidence against itself.

claims.statement: No single-variable polynomial sequence of degree >= 2 has an admissible Ford-Maynard triple. For A = {f(x)}, |J| = Q^{1/d}, so c = 1 - 1/d >= 1/2 for every d >= 2, and [FM] p.7's 'one can only hope for (II) for theta > c' collides with (1.1)'s theta < 1/2. Computed by x2plus1.exponents.ford_maynard_theta, which returns a range at d = 1 and raises for every d >= 2.
claims.notes: Same inferential status as the d = 2 case it generalises: [FM] state the ingredients and never draw the conclusion, and 'one can only hope' is an informal remark inside their discussion of the family P_theta. This is a claim about what the Type I/II framework can EXPRESS, never about whether any of these polynomials takes infinitely many prime values.

claims.statement: Proposition L.1. For n1 != n2 with d = gcd, n1 = da, n2 = db, the shared moduli correspond exactly to solutions of the conic b x^2 - a y^2 = a - b (proved: algebra). Solutions fall into classes, each an orbit under the fundamental norm-one unit eps of the relevant real quadratic order, so consecutive moduli satisfy m'/m -> eps^2 >= phi^4 = 6.8541 > 2 and a dyadic window holds at most one per class. The CLASS COUNT, however, is not bounded: Dickson gives 2^{omega(|a-b|)+O(1)} = O_eps(|a-b|^eps), so the proposition yields G'(n1,n2) << |n1-n2|^eps on a window and NOT the measured constant 2. eps >= phi^2 = 2.618033989 verified for every non-square discriminant < 5000, with the minimum attained at Delta = 5 -- which IS the pair (n1,n2) = (1,5) that attains the full graph's maximum. Window sweep: max Gram = 2 at every dyadic M from 128 to 8192 at X = 32000.
claims.notes: CORRECTED. The spacing half stands; the 'bounded by the number of classes, and the number of classes is small' half does not. Dickson, Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (1929), sec.46 pp.73-75 and sec.71 p.115, bounds primitive classes by 2^r (4 not | M), 2^{r+1}, 2^{r+2} with r = #odd primes | M -- unbounded. Located and read by a parallel session; SECOND-HAND here until this repo opens Dickson. The constant that bounds the spacing and the pair that attains the maximum are the same object, which is the reason to believe the mechanism rather than the number. What is still missing is a bound on the NUMBER of classes -- classical, not read here, and not asserted from memory. Also x'/x -> eps is asymptotic: the first two solutions of a class can sit closer, which is exactly how (1189, 71978) puts m = 65 and 109 in one window from two different classes.

claims.statement: Chowla's assertion sum_{n<=x} lambda(P(n)) = o(x), for the LIOUVILLE function lambda, is 'wide open for any polynomials with nonlinear irreducible factors' (Teravainen p.2). The theta -> 0 endpoint of Note F's Question F is the same statement for the MOBIUS function, |sum_{x<=X} mu(x^2+1)| << X (log X)^{-A}. For this sequence the trivial bound has never been beaten by any amount, at any level, signed or absolute.
claims.citation: Teravainen, arXiv:2010.07924v4, pp.1-2 (equation (1.1) and the sentence following)
claims.notes: Located by a parallel session, then fetched and read here before recording. This is the scoping fact that stops Question F being read as 'an estimate someone could plausibly supply'. It says nothing about whether x^2+1 is prime infinitely often. PRECISION, added on a sweep of the source: Teravainen's paper never mentions the Mobius function -- it is about lambda throughout, and (1.1) is stated for lambda. This repo needs mu. The two are universally regarded as equivalent in difficulty and are related by lambda = 1_square * mu, but THAT TRANSFER IS NOT CARRIED OUT HERE and openness for lambda does not logically imply openness for mu. What is quoted is therefore: the lambda statement is wide open. What the repo asserts on its own account is that the mu statement at the same endpoint is no easier. Note also that Teravainen's POSITIVE results (Thm 2.6, Cor 2.7) are for general bounded multiplicative g and so do cover mu; it is only the openness remark that is lambda-specific.

claims.statement: Bombieri-Vinogradov in the absolute-value norm -- sum_{q~Q} max_{(a,q)=1} |Delta(f,x;q,a)| << x/(log x)^A for Q <= x^{1/2}/(log x)^B -- is KNOWN for f = mu on the density-1 sequence: 'The analogous result is known to hold when f = mu, the Mobius function'. So absolute values are not intrinsically hopeless; it is the composition with a quadratic that kills them here.
claims.citation: Granville-Shao, arXiv:1703.06865v2, p.2 (display (1.1) and the sentence following)
claims.notes: Scopes difficulty-is-the-absolute-values, which was stated too broadly. Located by a parallel session, read here at source before recording.

claims.statement: n -> mu(n^2+1) is not a multiplicative function of n. It fails normalisation at n = 1 (mu(2) = -1, not 1) and fails non-degenerately at coprime (a,b) = (2,7), (2,9), (2,11). Hence Granville-Shao's theory of Bombieri-Vinogradov for multiplicative functions, and multiplicative-function machinery generally, is inapplicable AS STATED rather than merely too weak.
claims.notes: Trivial to verify and worth having as a test, because 'the multiplicative machinery is too weak here' and 'the multiplicative machinery does not apply here' are different statements and only the second is true.

claims.statement: With M = Q^theta and X = Q^{1/2} = |A|, Note H's S_mu(M) ~ sqrt(MX) gives a saving over the trivial bound of sqrt(X/M) = Q^{(1/2-theta)/2}: a power saving for every theta < 1/2, exactly zero at theta = 1/2. [ASP]'s (B1) requires M >= sqrt(x) = X, i.e. theta >= 1/2; [FM]'s (1.1) requires theta < 1/2. So the mu-cancellation holds on precisely the range Ford-Maynard admits and vanishes at precisely the point the asymptotic sieve's bilinear hypothesis begins. theta = 1/2 is where M = |A|, mean degree 1, kappa = 1 -- the forest.
claims.notes: The exponent arithmetic is elementary; what makes this `inferred` is that it rests on sqrt-MX-law, which is `extrapolated`. No new number is derived -- the content is only that the two windows the repo had been quoting are complements. It explains why the repo kept getting two answers about whether the mu-sum has a saving.

claims.statement: CONDITIONAL. If [FM]'s (II) could be weakened from arbitrary bounded xi_m, kappa_n to arbitrary xi_m with kappa_n = mu(n), the measured law would supply a Type II range on any [theta, theta+nu] inside [0, 1/2), placing x^2+1 at (gamma, theta, nu) = (1/2, 0, nu) for nu < 1/2 -- above Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec's (1/2, 0, 1/3) in [FM] Table 1.
claims.notes: NOT a claim that any FM theorem applies -- substituting a weaker hypothesis into a theorem is not valid reasoning. The content is where the parameters land. CORRECTION: an earlier version added 'inside the region their Theorem 2.5 (p.7) handles for divisor-bounded weights, which this sequence's indicator is'. STRUCK -- see fm-divisor-bounded-class-is-dense. FM p.13 (4.1) restricts C_bd to pairs satisfying BOTH |w_n| <= tau(n)^rho AND sum_p b_p >= x/(rho log x), and those cannot both hold at density x^{1/2}. Removing that support does not touch the conditional, which only ever claimed where the parameters land. The two blockers are unchanged: the mu-Type II as a theorem (its easiest endpoint is chowla-for-x2plus1-is-open) and a sieve needing only mu-coefficients (Note F proves the specialised result cannot upgrade here).

claims.statement: PROPOSED AND FALSE. Since kappa = |B|^2 for A_B = {a + b^2 i : b in B}, the kappa criterion is met at |B| = 2 while Merikoski's sparse-set theorem needs |B| >> Y^{1-delta}; the conjecture was that the incidence graph stays C4-free until |B| is a positive power of Q, so that kappa is wrong by an exponent.
claims.notes: Refuted by direct construction: 4-cycles exist at |B| = 2 with both artefacts controlled. Recorded because it is exactly the kind of plausible idea that recurs -- it reads like a corollary of 'kappa is necessary, not sufficient' and is not one. Two measurements supported it before the controls were applied, and both were artefacts (unit cofactor; commensurable lines).

claims.statement: For A_B = {a + b^2 i : b in B}, kappa = |B|^2 exactly, and 4-cycles appear at |B| = 2 -- the same threshold. Verified with both artefacts excluded: B = {2,3} (so 1 not in B and neither b divides the other, killing the dilation z -> (b2/b1)^2 z), cofactor floor N(n) >= N(m) (killing the unit column). Explicit: n1 = 4+2i, n2 = 19+7i share m = 1+4i and m = 2+6i, all four products associates of elements of A_{2,3}. A parallel session obtained ~300 collisions for each of B = {2,3},{2,5},{3,5},{3,4} against ~600 for the leaky {1,2},{1,3}.
claims.notes: So kappa must NOT be demoted for being off by an exponent -- it is sharp at the threshold for this family. 'Necessary, not sufficient' stands on the a^2+(b^2+1)^2 control, which is about how much kappa buys ABOVE the threshold, not about where the threshold is. Was PROSE in the `experiment` field, which the registry's rule for `rigorous_finite` -- "`experiment` naming the script" -- does not admit; the parallel session's guard found it. exp23 computes it, and it reproduces exactly.

claims.statement: C4-freeness forces sum_n C(d_n,2) <= C(R,2). At Q = 10^6 the x^2+1 graph sits far below that ceiling -- col-side ratio 0.048, 0.016, 0.005 on windows [16,64), [64,256), [256,1024) -- i.e. 20x to 400x fewer edges than C4-freeness would permit. a^2+b^4 gives 29.0, 7.71, 1.95 on the same windows, exceeding 1 as it must. So the lemma is nowhere near binding as an edge count: the graph is far sparser than C4-freeness requires, and the cycles that appear once a second line is added are created by arithmetic rather than by density.
claims.notes: Explains why a density statistic like kappa cannot locate the threshold: the constraint that bites is not an edge count. The a^2+b^4 row is the control that the measure detects the difference at all. Was PROSE in the `experiment` field, which the registry's rule for `rigorous_finite` -- "`experiment` naming the script" -- does not admit; the parallel session's guard found it. exp23 computes it, and it reproduces exactly. AND THIS IS WHY NOTE F GIVES A THEOREM WHERE THE NOTE O BOUNDS LEAVE GAPS -- a connection neither note drew. Note F's lemma is not a size argument: (x1+i)(x4+i) = u(x2+i)(x3+i) forces the PRODUCT and the SUM of the two x's simultaneously, so the pair is determined, and nothing in it compares a magnitude to a threshold. Every bound in the Note O apparatus is a size argument -- |V| against M/sqrt(3D), ratios against a window, products against (MD)^{4/3} -- and `size-bounds-permit-far-more-than-occurs-at-every-scale` measures the consequence at three scales: the admissible set is far larger than the realised one, every time. So the same distinction this claim draws between arithmetic and density explains the difference between the two halves of the repo's own work: the arithmetic statement closes, the size statements bound. It also says what a proof of O.2 would have to look like -- not a sharper constant, since sharpening moves the admissible set and not the realised one, but an arithmetic obstruction of Note F's kind.

claims.statement: DFI Lemma 2 (p.436) instantiated at X = |A| = Q^{1/2}: (27) holds with gamma(d) = 2 rho(d)/d, (29) with c = 4, and G(z) = prod_{p<z}(1+gamma(p)) ~ log z (one power). Its error X G(z)^2 (2^{-log(D/z)/log w} + c K^{-1} log y) is o(|A|/log Q) once D >= z exp(C (log log Q)^2) and w >= (log Q)^4 -- quasi-polynomial in log Q, not a power, so Lemma 2 costs essentially nothing in level. But it requires D > z ('3 <= K <= w < y < z < D'), and Note B caps D at o(Q^{1/2}); hence z = o(Q^{1/2}). So Lemma 2's REACH IS CAPPED AT P_2: at no admissible parameter choice can the quantity it computes distinguish a prime from a product of two primes. Prime detection needs z ~ Q^{1/2}, i.e. D > Q^{1/2}, which Note B forbids.
claims.citation: Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec, Ann. of Math. 141 (1995), Lemma 2 p.436, hypotheses (27) and (29) p.435; bilinear forms (32),(33) p.436
claims.notes: REFUTED the same day it was written, on reading DFI's page images rather than the scan's OCR layer. Both claims rested on 'prime detection needs sieving to z > Q^{1/2}'. DFI do not sieve that way: Lemma 3 removes the p,q terms BILINEARLY -- that is the point of the identity -- and Theorem S runs with z <= x^{1/2-eps}. The P_2 ceiling is a fact about classical sieves and Lemma 2 is not one. There is no level deficit; see dfi-theorem-S-typeI-met-typeII-not.

claims.statement: 'There is no single non-linear polynomial for which we would know the answer for Schinzel's conjecture, even for k = 1. However, if primes are substituted by almost primes, then Schinzel's conjecture is true in case of k = 1 for an arbitrary polynomial f.' So: primes unknown for EVERY degree >= 2, almost-primes known for every degree -- the degree-uniform phenomenon that Note L's degree ladder supplies a mechanism for.
claims.citation: Pintz, 'Landau's problems on primes', J. Theor. Nombres Bordeaux 21 (2009), p.5; hierarchy at section 19
claims.notes: Pintz states the phenomenon degree-uniformly and states no mechanism. Note L supplies a mechanism (alpha = 1/d, kappa = X^{2-d}, no Ford-Maynard triple for d >= 2) and no phenomenon. Neither substitutes for the other, and the ladder should not be described as explaining Pintz's sentence -- it is consistent with it, which is weaker.

claims.statement: Step 2 checkpoint, unit 1 of 3. Through DFI Lemma 2, prime detection needs the sieving level z > Q^{1/2} (a survivor of norm <= Q with no prime factor below Q^{1/2} is prime) and Lemma 2 requires D > z, hence D > Q^{1/2}. Note B gives sum_{d<=D}|r_d| ~ D, so (R)'s A(x)(log x)^{-222} forces D << Q^{1/2}(log Q)^{-222}. The deficit is a factor of (log Q)^{222}: a fixed LOG-POWER, not a power of Q.
claims.notes: REFUTED the same day it was written, on reading DFI's page images rather than the scan's OCR layer. Both claims rested on 'prime detection needs sieving to z > Q^{1/2}'. DFI do not sieve that way: Lemma 3 removes the p,q terms BILINEARLY -- that is the point of the identity -- and Theorem S runs with z <= x^{1/2-eps}. The P_2 ceiling is a fact about classical sieves and Lemma 2 is not one. There is no level deficit; see dfi-theorem-S-typeI-met-typeII-not.

claims.statement: THEOREM S (p.437): for C = {c_n}, 1 <= n <= x, bounded by tau(n), if (34) R(D) << x(log x)^{-2} holds with D = x^{1/2-eps} and (35) R(w,y) << x(log x)^{-10} holds with y = x^{1/3-eps}, w = x^{(log log x)^{-3}}, then sum_{p<=x} c_p << eps*pi(x). Here R(D) = sum_{d<D} lambda_d sum_m c_{dm} is the SPECIAL bilinear form and R(w,y) = sum_{w<n<y} beta_n sum_{(m,n)=1} alpha_m c_{mn} the GENERAL one, with |alpha_m| <= omega(m), |beta_n| <= 1, |lambda_d| <= 1, and 'in our case, beta_n will be supported on primes'. Restated relative to |A| = Q^{1/2}: (34) becomes Type I at level Q^{1/2-eps}, which Note B PERMITS (D << Q^{1/2}(log Q)^{-222}); (35) becomes Type II with the short variable up to Q^{1/3-eps}, which is Note J's object and is NOT available. The level is not the obstruction.
claims.citation: Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec, Ann. of Math. 141 (1995): Theorem S and (34),(35) p.437; Lemma 3 p.437; Prop. 2 p.426; Lemma 2 p.436
claims.notes: Read from 300 dpi page images; the scan's OCR layer is unusable (it renders Prop 2's bound as 'N4M3+'). Confirmed from outside: Ford-Maynard's Table 1 places DFI at (gamma,theta,nu) = (1/2, 0, 1/3), and theta+nu = 1/3 is exactly Theorem S's y = x^{1/3-eps}. Two papers read separately, same triple. NOTE ALSO that Theorem S's conclusion is an UPPER bound -- it is an equidistribution tool and would not detect primes even if both hypotheses were met. And the scale-freeness stops at Lemma 2: Lemma 3 and Theorem S fix c_n <= tau(n), X << x log x, i.e. density one, so there is no re-normalisation of Theorem S, only an analogue that must be re-proved.

claims.statement: PROPOSITION 2 (p.426): 'Suppose beta_n are supported on primes. For h << MN we have (10) B(M,N) << ||alpha rho|| ||beta|| (M^{1/2} + N^{3/4} M^{3/8+eps}).' Only beta is restricted, not alpha. The 3/8 is an exponent inside a bound, NOT a range for the modulus -- DFI's Type II window is fixed by Theorem S at y = x^{1/3-eps}.
claims.citation: Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec, Ann. of Math. 141 (1995), Proposition 2 p.426
claims.notes: Corrects two things at once. An earlier reading here, off the broken OCR, said 'alpha, beta are supported on primes' -- wrong, and it contradicted the repo's own correct record from p.437. And Note J's X^{3/4} moduli range was derived by reading the 3/8 as a window; the correct range is Q^{1/3-eps} in the short variable.

claims.statement: For A_B = {a + b^2 i : b in B} the kappa criterion and C4-freeness both fire at |B| = 2 (kappa = 4). The best available METHOD needs |B| >= X^{1/2-delta}, i.e. B within X^delta of the whole available range: Merikoski Thm 1.2, 'for all B subset [eta X^{1/2}, (1-eta) X^{1/2}] with |B| >= X^{1/2-delta} we have sum_{p=a^2+b^2<=X} 1_B(b) >>_eps X^{1/2-eps}|B|'. So kappa > 1 is satisfied a FULL POWER OF X before any method applies -- kappa = 4 against kappa = X^{1-2delta}. That is the quantitative content of 'necessary, not sufficient', on the method axis rather than the graph axis.
claims.citation: Merikoski, On Gaussian primes in sparse sets, arXiv:2302.11331v3, Thm 1.2 p.2 (Compositio Math. 161 (2025) 181-243)
claims.notes: Status is `inferred`, not `quoted`: Merikoski's threshold is a quote and lives in `merikoski-sparse-sets-off-chart`, but the COMPARISON with kappa = 4 rests on two `rigorous_finite` claims of ours, and the dependency guard rejected the quoted version -- correctly, since a quote cannot rest on a measurement. This is what the refuted `kappa-off-by-an-exponent` was reaching for, and it shows why that conjecture failed: it tested the incidence GRAPH, which is innocent -- 4-cycles really do appear at |B| = 2 -- when the power-of-X gap is on the METHOD axis. Merikoski notes his is the first unconditional power saving in the density of B at all; before it, Fouvry-Iwaniec needed density (log X)^{-C}.

claims.statement: DFI state that the parity-breaking input IS the arbitrary-coefficient bilinear form. p.425: 'It is now well-understood that information about L_d(M) is not sufficient to demonstrate asymptotic formulae for primes (or even their existence) due to a "parity problem" [B]. In recent years this problem has been partially surmounted by adding new information about general bilinear forms of the type (8) B(M,N) = sum sum_{(m,n)=1} alpha_m beta_n rho_h(mn). HERE alpha_m AND beta_n ARE ARBITRARY BUT BOUNDED COMPLEX NUMBERS with support M < m <= 2M and N < n <= 2N. In this paper we are able to obtain just barely enough information about the sums L_d(M) and B(M,N) to wipe out the parity problem in its entirety.' Note F proves that object has no cancellation for A = {x+i}.
claims.citation: Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec, Ann. of Math. 141 (1995), p.425 (immediately above Proposition 1), read from page images
claims.notes: This places Note F much more sharply than 'dispersion has no main term': Note F is the statement that DFI's PARITY-BREAKING INPUT DOES NOT EXIST for this sequence. Found by the parallel session and verified here from the images independently. Note also what they NEED (arbitrary coefficients, (8)) versus what they PROVE (Prop. 2, beta on primes) -- the same gap [FM] footnote 1 expects to close in general and Note F shows cannot close here. Their 'plausible' bounds on the same page are L_d(M) << M^{1/2}(hdM)^eps and B(M,N) << ||alpha|| ||beta|| (M+N)^{1/2}(hMN)^eps, against Prop. 1's achieved L_d(M) << (h,d)^{1/20}(d/M)^{1/20}M^{1+eps}.

claims.statement: factorization.admissible_roots_upto builds the full table of roots of r^2+1 = 0 (mod q) for all admissible q <= Q_max in bulk (SPF sieve, one sqrt(-1) per prime p = 1 mod 4 lifted by Hensel, CRT along each q). It agrees with roots_of_minus_one exactly for q <= 3000, and gives sum_q rho(q)/Q = 0.47744 at Q = 10^6 against the predicted 3/(2 pi) = 0.47746. That is Note B's calibration constant, reproduced from an unrelated code path -- Note B measures it by enumerating Gaussian ideals, this by counting roots of a congruence.
claims.notes: Written to lift Note J's all-moduli cross-check off its X <= 10^5 cap, which was sympy's factorint per modulus rather than anything mathematical. Reaches Q = 10^6 in 0.9s. The agreement with 3/(2 pi) to five digits is the check that it is the same object as the Type I harness's.

claims.statement: Xiannan Li attributes the density limit to Type II: 'The second, sometimes referred to as Type II estimates, involves bounds on certain bilinear sums attached to these sequences. Achieving the latter type of estimate is the most difficult part and is the ingredient which breaks the parity barrier.' Two factors govern it: sparsity, and whether a lattice restriction is available -- 'it is crucial that these sequences are all special values of norm forms of some number field ... for certain homogeneous polynomials, such as a^3 + 2b^3, estimating the bilinear sum involves a restriction of a variable to a one dimensional lattice, and this makes the problem more tractable.' And the boundary: 'Both the asymptotic sieve for primes from Friedlander and Iwaniec and Harman's alternative sieve as used in Heath-Brown's work fail to prove asymptotic estimates for sequences with exponential density strictly lower than 2/3.' The numerical limit is separate: his footnote 1 says a 7/12 primes-in-short-intervals exponent caps the region width at 5/67, giving density 2/3 - 5/201 = 0.641791.
claims.citation: Xiannan Li, Prime values of a sparse polynomial sequence, arXiv:2111.05403v1, p.2 and footnote 1 p.3
claims.notes: Discharges the last [VERIFY] in the repo. Two consequences: the norm-form condition IS met by x^2+1 = N(x+i), which is Note A, so what this sequence lacks is the second item -- the lattice restriction, which needs a variable to restrict. That is Note L's two-parameter freedom named from inside the technique rather than from the exponents. The repo previously carried 0.6418 from memory; it is 2/3 - 5/201 exactly.

claims.statement: Over EVERY reduced ratio class (y^2+1)/(x^2+1): at X = 3000, 2014 classes have >= 2 shared moduli, of which 1636 put at most one modulus in a dyadic window and 378 put two -- and NONE puts three. At X = 6000: 3916 classes, 3167 / 749 / ZERO. Exact orbit grouping (union-find under A, A^-1 and x -> -x) shows populated-orbit counts 1005, 891, 27, 4, 1 for 1..5 orbits, so classes with three or more populated orbits DO occur and still never put three moduli in a window.
claims.notes: REFUTES a tempting reformulation that both sessions reached: 'two moduli in one window must come from two different classes'. FALSE. (n1,n2) = (2,85), conic 85x^2-2y^2 = -83, solutions (11,72) and (15,98) give m = 61 and 113, ratio 1.85 < 2, and A^-1(11,72) = (-15,98): the two differ by the IMPROPER automorph x -> -x, which is not in {+-A^k} but which m = (x^2+1)/n1 cannot see. So one class-up-to-conjugation can supply two moduli in a window, and 202 of the 378 classes attaining window-max 2 at X = 3000 are exactly that case. The proper-class spacing explains one modulus per proper class; the improper pairing explains a second; NOTHING explains the absence of a third.

claims.statement: Three moduli in one dyadic window is exactly m_{i+2}/m_i < 2. Over every ratio class: at X = 1500, 3000, 5000 the minimum CONSECUTIVE ratio falls 1.0783, 1.0547, 1.0412 while the minimum TWO-STEP ratio is pinned at exactly 13.0000, attained at (a,b) = (1,85) with m = 2, 17, 26, as the triple count doubles from 55 to 109. The lower tail is a cluster, not an approach: the nine smallest two-step ratios at X = 5000 are 13.00, 14.50, 14.80, 14.90, 15.16, 16.40, 17.06, 17.55, 18.02, and the next is 32.5 -- nothing in (18.02, 32.5), nothing below 13, median 819. And ALL twenty smallest have a = 1, i.e. n1 | n2, so the extremal object is the conic y^2 - b x^2 = b - 1. RESTRICTED to pairs a Type II split can actually meet -- both cofactors >= 2, since a = 1 with d = 1 is the unit cofactor -- the floor is 73.0000 at (a,b) = (5,481) for X = 1500, 2500, 3500 and steps down to 66.4923 at (5,4033) at X = 5000 -- a margin of 33x over the threshold 2 rather than 6.5x, but NOT pinned the way the unrestricted 13 is. Window maximum is 2 in both populations.
claims.notes: EXTENDED TO X = 8000 with the unanchored (ratio) criterion: 12,923,483 ratio classes, 110 informative (>= 3 shared moduli), 1000 classes putting two moduli in one window, ZERO putting three -- and the minimum two-step ratio is STILL exactly 13.0000, at (1,85) with moduli 2, 17, 26. So the floor is unmoved from X = 1500 through 8000 while the informative population more than doubles, which is the stability the earlier three sizes could only suggest. The nearest miss is a factor 6.50 from what a window needs. DENOMINATOR: 110 informative classes, not 12.9 million -- a class with fewer than three shared moduli is silent on the question. POPULATION CORRECTION: the global minimiser (a,b) = (1,85) has M/sqrt(D) = 84/sqrt(85) = 9.111, BELOW the triple threshold 11.484, so it could never have held a triple at all -- nor could (1,5) at 1.789, (1,65) at 7.938, or (5,481) at 9.706. Restricted to triple-capable classes the minimum two-step ratio at X = 3000 is 14.50 at (1,533) with m = 10, 122, 145, over 23 such classes. So 13.0000 and the triple question are about different populations and must not be quoted as one. SUPERSEDED IN INTERPRETATION, not in numbers. Note O's Prop O.1 gives a two-step bound of 2 outright, so 13.0000 and 66.4923 are SEARCH EXTREMA, not floors, and the restricted one should keep drifting down -- 73 -> 66.5 is the start of that. Note O also predicts the step: (5,4033) first becomes visible at X = 4175, between the 3500 and 5000 sweeps where it appeared. The empty bin that prompted the search was real evidence FOR a mechanism but was not itself the mechanism. A gap of 6.5x, stable in X, with an empty bin below it. Both sessions independently built a probability model predicting three-in-a-window should be merely improbable; this refutes it -- improbability does not pin a minimum at 13.0000 across a doubling of the sample. The reduction the floor points at is a GAP PRINCIPLE separating distinct proper classes of a fixed binary quadratic form; neither session has the citation. The extremal triple is not three near-coincident solutions but a tight pair (m = 17, 26, ratio 1.53) plus a distant third (m = 2). The a = 1 concentration is structural, not a counting artefact: 59 triples exist with a >= 2 and their floor is five times higher. So a gap principle covering only the a = 1 family y^2 + 1 = b(x^2+1) would settle the extremal case but not the case the sieve meets, where the margin is wider. CAUTION recorded rather than smoothed: the two floors are different kinds of evidence. The unrestricted 13 is pinned across four sizes while the triple count doubles. The restricted floor held at 73 for three sizes then stepped to 66.5. One 9% step is not a drift toward the threshold, but it is not a pinned minimum either, and an earlier draft stated 66.5 as though it were.

claims.statement: The close-pair modulus ratio equals tau^2 with tau = (sqrt b + sqrt a)/(sqrt b - sqrt a). Over all 304 close pairs at X = 2500 the median relative error is 2.4e-05 and only 2 exceed 1% (the error is O(1/m), so the outliers are the smallest moduli). The threshold is sharp: tau^2 < 2 requires b/a > 33.97, and the minimum b/a over those 304 pairs is 34.1 -- attained, never violated. But tau alone does NOT forbid a third: that needs tau^4 < 2, i.e. b/a > 134.3, and the median b/a over close pairs is 148.2. And the multiplier can act twice in one class: at X = 2500, 302 classes have exactly one close pair and (a,b) = (1,53) has two -- m = 10, 17, 24650, 42850, ratios 1.700 and 1.7383 = tau^2. What never happens is two at CONSECUTIVE positions.
claims.experiment: experiments/exp13_window_gap.py; tau check in-session against exp12_tau_multiplier's law
claims.notes: Independent verification of Note O's multiplier, done from its docstring without reading the note. The (1,53) case matters for how Note O is phrased: 'the multiplier acts at most once' is false per class and true per consecutive triple, which is what the proof actually needs.

claims.statement: For a close pair of shared moduli, V = X_i Y_j - X_j Y_i satisfies |V| ~ (M/(2 sqrt D))(sqrt r - 1/sqrt r) with r = m_j/m_i, M = b-a, D = ab. At X = 4000 the histogram of |V| over 498 close pairs is {2: 495, 24: 1, 66: 1, 182: 1}, and the three non-2 values are the asymptotic working, not failing: predicted 24.0, 65.7, 174.6 against observed 24, 66, 182 (relative error 0.001, 0.005, 0.041). Their M/sqrt(D) is 89.3, 227.4, 650.5 against a median of 11.96 over all close pairs and a threshold of 5.657 for |V| >= 2; the |V| = 2 population itself runs from M/sqrt(D) = 5.6666 to 87.0. So |V| = 2 is not a lemma with three exceptions -- |V| is whatever the asymptotic gives, and it equals 2 for pairs near the minimal-separation configuration, which is most of them.
claims.notes: The V histogram and the asymptotic comparison were run in-session against exp13's ratio_classes; exp13 itself reports the window and two-step statistics rather than V. Bears on Note O's Proposition O.1. If its step (i) derives P = Q^2 from |V| = 2 -- which gives U = +-(a+b) -- then it covers only that case, and the general one has |V| = 2k with U^2 = M^2 + 4k^2 D, a different factorisation. Also proved here by parity: for a, b both odd, X_k = Y_k (mod 2) since m odd makes both even and m even makes both odd, so V is always even and |V| = 1 is impossible. That much IS a lemma.
